claims.text: Dermatology AI fails in dark-skin, non-cancer settings.
claims.poster_quote: Dermatology AI fails in dark-skin, non-cancer settings.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: When such models underperform, the field has largely attributed the failure to skin-tone underrepresentation.
claims.reason: Introduction section states that dermatology AI models underperform in settings with darker skin and non-cancerous conditions.

claims.text: Disease shift may matter more than skin tone underrepresentation.
claims.poster_quote: Disease shift may matter more than skin tone underrepresentation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In our setting, disease-distribution shift contributes more than skin tone: the cancer baseline degrades sharply from its in-domain performance to unfamiliar conditions (a drop from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy across clinical categories), a far larger effect than the within-disease skin-tone gap, which is comparatively small (0.10-0.18) and did not show a consistent direction.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly states that disease-distribution shift dominates over skin tone underrepresentation.

claims.text: Models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data are deployed where patients have darker skin and non-cancerous conditions like eczema or tinea.
claims.poster_quote: Models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data are deployed where patients have darker skin and non-cancerous conditions like eczema or tinea.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Patients present with more pigmented skin, and with a disease burden dominated by inflammatory and infectious conditions (eczema, tinea, impetigo, scabies) that are largely absent from cancer-centric training data.
claims.reason: Introduction section describes the deployment context where patients have darker skin and non-cancerous conditions.

claims.text: Distribution shift causes bigger drops than tone gaps.
claims.poster_quote: Distribution shift causes bigger drops than tone gaps.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In our setting, disease-distribution shift contributes more than skin tone: the cancer baseline degrades sharply from its in-domain performance to unfamiliar conditions (a drop from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy across clinical categories), a far larger effect than the within-disease skin-tone gap, which is comparatively small (0.10-0.18) and did not show a consistent direction.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 confirms that distribution shift causes larger performance drops than tone gaps.

claims.text: Table 2 shows 0.62→0.21 drop for cancer baseline on SCIN.
claims.poster_quote: Table 2 shows 0.62→0.21 drop for cancer baseline on SCIN.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The cancer baseline is strong in-domain (0.62) but degrades sharply on unfamiliar conditions (0.21 across categories; 0.06 at fine granularity).
claims.reason: Table 2 and Section 4.1 report the 0.62 to 0.21 drop for the cancer baseline on SCIN.

claims.text: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions.
claims.poster_quote: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions (+0.06 purity lift), while dermatology models retain transferable structure (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On its home domain, the cancer baseline has the strongest representational structure of any model (purity lift +0.42), yet on SCIN its features barely separate conditions (+0.06) close to chance, demonstrating a genuine representational deficit rather than a missing output head.
claims.reason: Section 4.2 explicitly states that label-free analysis reveals a representational collapse for cancer features on unfamiliar conditions.

claims.text: Cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions with a +0.06 purity lift.
claims.poster_quote: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions (+0.06 purity lift), while dermatology models retain transferable structure (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On its home domain, the cancer baseline has the strongest representational structure of any model (purity lift +0.42), yet on SCIN its features barely separate conditions (+0.06) close to chance, demonstrating a genuine representational deficit rather than a missing output head.
claims.reason: Section 4.2 confirms the cancer baseline's features collapse to near-chance with a +0.06 purity lift on SCIN.

claims.text: Dermatology models retain transferable structure with a DermLIP +0.23 purity lift.
claims.poster_quote: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions (+0.06 purity lift), while dermatology models retain transferable structure (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Dermatology foundation models retain three to four times more transferable structure under the same unfamiliar conditions (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.reason: Section 4.2 explicitly states that DermLIP retains transferable structure with a +0.23 purity lift.

claims.text: Representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).
claims.poster_quote: Representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Across models, recoverable performance closely tracks the label-free representation quality of Fig. 2 (r = 0.90 between SCIN purity lift and full-probe balanced accuracy across the four models).
claims.reason: Section 4.3 explicitly states that representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).

claims.text: Use dermatology foundation models, not cancer ones.
claims.poster_quote: Use dermatology foundation models, not cancer ones.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: First, model selection may matter more than local retraining: since recoverable performance is bounded by representation quality, teams may benefit from starting with a dermatology-pretrained foundation model rather than a cancer-specialized classifier.
claims.reason: Section 6 recommends using dermatology foundation models over cancer-specialized ones for deployment.

claims.text: Adapt with 10 examples/class; runs on CPU.
claims.poster_quote: Adapt with 10 examples/class; runs on CPU.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Second, modest labeling may suffice: a few-shot probe with roughly ten labeled examples per local category recovered most attainable performance in our experiments, suggesting a clinic could adapt a model with a small, locally curated label set. Third, the adaptation step itself is lightweight and runs on CPU.
claims.reason: Section 6 confirms adaptation with 10 examples/class and that it runs on CPU.

claims.text: Table 3 confirms recovery.
claims.poster_quote: Table 3 confirms recovery.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Table 3 reports low-compute adaptation on SCIN categories.
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms recovery results for low-compute adaptation.

claims.text: We test four frozen models on two datasets using linear probing, kNN, and few-shot adaptation.
claims.poster_quote: We test four frozen models on two datasets using linear probing, kNN, and few-shot adaptation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For each (model, dataset) pair we extract frozen embeddings and evaluate with three analyses. (1) Linear probing. (2) Label-free representation quality. (3) Low-compute adaptation.
claims.reason: Section 3.3 describes testing four frozen models on two datasets using linear probing, kNN, and few-shot adaptation.

claims.text: Fig. 1 shows the pipeline.
claims.poster_quote: Fig. 1 shows the pipeline.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Fig. 1. System architecture: four frozen models encode four public datasets into patient-level embeddings, evaluated by three complementary analyses.
claims.reason: Figure 1 shows the pipeline for the study.

claims.text: Models include cancer-trained ResNet-50, dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and general vision model DINOv3.
claims.poster_quote: Models include cancer-trained ResNet-50, dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and general vision model DINOv3.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We evaluate four models as frozen feature extractors: (i) a cancer baseline, ResNet-50 (ImageNet-initialized) fine-tuned on the pooled HAM10000+ISIC eight-class task, with the classification head removed to yield 2048-d features; (ii) DermLIP [4] (512-d) and (iii) MONET [5] (1024-d), open dermatology vision-language foundation models; and (iv) DINOv3 [13] (facebook/dinov3-vitb16-pretrain-lvd1689m, pooler output, 768-d), a general-purpose self-supervised vision model pretrained on natural images.
claims.reason: Section 3.2 lists the models used, including ResNet-50, DermLIP, MONET, and DINOv3.

claims.text: Experiments use patient-level splits and bootstrap CIs on free-tier compute.
claims.poster_quote: Experiments use patient-level splits and bootstrap CIs on free-tier compute.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: All experiments ran on free-tier cloud compute (a single Kaggle NVIDIA T4 GPU session plus CPU-only sessions), deliberately matching resource-limited constraints.
claims.reason: Section 3.3 confirms experiments used patient-level splits, bootstrap CIs, and free-tier compute.

claims.text: DDI tone gaps range from 0.10 to 0.18 and are inconsistent in direction.
claims.poster_quote: DDI tone gaps: 0.10–0.18, inconsistent direction
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: By contrast, the DDI tone gap is small (0.10-0.18) and inconsistent in direction; the cancer baseline’s worst group is the lightest, DINOv3’s the darkest, indicating no systematic monotonic tone bias.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 reports DDI tone gaps ranging from 0.10 to 0.18 and inconsistent in direction.

claims.paper_evidence: Few-shot probe with only ten labeled examples per category nearly matches or exceeds the full probe (DermLIP: 0.41 vs. 0.36).
claims.reason: Section 4.3 reports few-shot recovery for DermLIP to 0.41 compared to the cancer baseline's 0.19.
